obligations.obligation: Custodian must comply with a public records request (produce records or justify withholding in writing), not merely acknowledge it
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.21(b)
obligations.who_owes: Any City custodian of public records: HSH, DPH, Real Estate Division (City Administrator), Planning
obligations.deadline_rule: As soon as possible and within 10 days following receipt of the request. Note this is a compliance deadline, stronger than CPRA Gov. Code 7922.535(a), which only requires a determination in 10 days.
obligations.known_status: In force. SOTF found HSH in violation of 67.21(b) on 5/6/2026 (File No. 26035).

obligations.obligation: Custodian must provide, in writing, a statement of the existence, quantity, form and nature of records on a subject, and assist the requester in identifying records
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.21(c)
obligations.who_owes: Any City custodian of public records
obligations.deadline_rule: Within 7 days following receipt of the request, when requested to do so
obligations.known_status: In force. SOTF found HSH violated 67.21(c) on 5/6/2026 (File No. 26037) for failing to provide assistance.

obligations.obligation: Satisfy an Immediate Disclosure Request (IDR). Requires the words "Immediate Disclosure Request" across the top of the request AND on the envelope, subject line, or cover sheet.
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.25(a)
obligations.who_owes: Any City custodian of public records
obligations.deadline_rule: No later than close of business on the day following the day of the request
obligations.known_status: In force. DPH publishes it as "close of the next business day". SOTF File No. 26037 charged HSH under 67.25 for blowing an IDR.

obligations.obligation: If claiming an extension on an IDR (voluminous records, remote storage, need to consult another department), notify the requester in writing
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.25(b)
obligations.who_owes: Any City custodian of public records
obligations.deadline_rule: Notice due by close of business on the business day following the request. The ordinance text says the extension is 10 days and cites the repealed Gov. Code 6456.1/6256.1; SF departments in practice apply the modern CPRA 14-day cap under Gov. Code 7922.535(b). The mismatch is unresolved and worth flagging on the site.
obligations.known_status: In force with an obsolete cross-reference. DPH's own page states 14 calendar days.

obligations.obligation: Produce responsive records on a rolling/incremental basis rather than withholding everything until the full set is collected
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.25(d)
obligations.who_owes: City and County of San Francisco (all departments)
obligations.deadline_rule: Records must be produced as soon as possible by the end of the same business day they are reviewed and collected, when the requester asks for rolling production. Failure is expressly a violation of Article III.
obligations.known_status: In force. Underused lever: ask for rolling production explicitly in the request text so a bulk-delay response is itself a violation.

obligations.obligation: CPRA determination on whether the request seeks disclosable records, with reasons and an estimated date records will be available
obligations.legal_citation: Cal. Gov. Code Sec. 7922.535(a)
obligations.who_owes: Every state and local agency, including all SF departments
obligations.deadline_rule: Within 10 days of receipt of the request
obligations.known_status: In force (CPRA recodification of former Gov. Code 6253(c)).

obligations.obligation: CPRA extension in "unusual circumstances" requires written notice from the agency head or designee stating the reasons and the date a determination is expected
obligations.legal_citation: Cal. Gov. Code Sec. 7922.535(b)-(c)
obligations.who_owes: Every state and local agency, including all SF departments
obligations.deadline_rule: Extension may not exceed 14 days. Permitted grounds are limited to the six listed in subsection (c): records in field facilities, voluminous records, need to consult another agency or component, need to compile data or write a program, cyberattack blocking server access, and one further listed circumstance.
obligations.known_status: In force. An extension notice that does not name one of the (c) grounds is defective and is the cleanest thing for the tracker to flag.

obligations.obligation: Supervisor of Records (the City Attorney) must determine whether a withheld record is public, on petition by the requester
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.21(d), with "Supervisor of Records" defined as the City Attorney at Sec. 67.20(c)
obligations.who_owes: San Francisco City Attorney, Government Team
obligations.deadline_rule: As soon as possible and within 10 days of the petition. If the custodian then fails to comply with the resulting order within 5 days, the Supervisor of Records must notify the District Attorney or Attorney General.
obligations.known_status: Active. Petition by email to Supervisor.Records@sfcityatty.org. The City Attorney's own page states it does NOT decide whether responses are timely and does NOT issue violations, so it is the wrong forum for a blown deadline. 25 annual reports published, latest covering calendar 2024.

obligations.obligation: Sunshine Ordinance Task Force must determine whether a requested record is public, on petition/complaint
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.21(e)
obligations.who_owes: Sunshine Ordinance Task Force
obligations.deadline_rule: As soon as possible and within 2 days after its next meeting, but in no case later than 45 days from receipt of a written petition. On a determination that the record is public, SOTF must immediately order production; if the custodian fails to comply within 5 days, SOTF must notify the DA or AG.
obligations.known_status: Routinely missed. SOTF's own 2025 Annual Report: average 138 days to hear a complaint, only 25% scheduled within 45 days, backlog grew from 20 to 60 during 2025.

obligations.obligation: Requester may go to court or to the Ethics Commission for enforcement and penalties if no City or State official has taken enforcement action
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.35(d)
obligations.who_owes: Right accrues to the requester; obligation falls on Ethics Commission / courts
obligations.deadline_rule: 40 days after a complaint is filed with no enforcement action taken
obligations.known_status: Contested. Ethics took "no action" on the SOTF referral in Lotocki v. SFPD (File No. 24021) on 7/11/2025, questioning whether it has authority to impose penalties on SOTF referrals at all. Ethics staff proposed 2025 regulation revisions that SOTF says would gut 67.35(d).

obligations.obligation: Willful failure by an elected official, department head, or managerial employee to discharge Sunshine/Brown Act/CPRA duties is official misconduct, handled by the Ethics Commission
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.34
obligations.who_owes: Ethics Commission (adjudication); elected officials and department heads (duty)
obligations.deadline_rule: No deadline in the section. Ethics Section 10(A) hearings cover alleged willful violations by elected officials or department heads; Section 10(B) covers everyone else and non-willful violations by department heads.
obligations.known_status: Weak in practice. "Willful" has never been defined by Ethics despite repeated SOTF requests. SOTF made only 2 willful and 1 non-willful referral in all of 2025.

obligations.obligation: Any person may sue for injunctive relief, declaratory relief, or writ of mandate to enforce access, with mandatory costs and attorney fees to a prevailing plaintiff
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.35(a)-(c)
obligations.who_owes: Superior Court jurisdiction; City pays fees on loss
obligations.deadline_rule: No administrative exhaustion required. Sec. 67.21(f) confirms the administrative remedy does not limit judicial remedies. Sec. 67.21(g) puts the burden on the custodian to prove the exemption with specificity.
obligations.known_status: In force. This is the only remedy in Chapter 67 with real teeth.

obligations.obligation: Supervisor of Records must publish a tally and report of every petition brought before it, including the record sought, the custodian, the ruling, whether it was overturned, and whether orders were followed
obligations.legal_citation: SF Admin. Code Sec. 67.21(h)
obligations.who_owes: San Francisco City Attorney (Supervisor of Records)
obligations.deadline_rule: At least annually, and as otherwise requested by SOTF
obligations.known_status: Published. 25 reports listed; the most recent covers January 1 to December 31, 2024 (25th Annual Report). The 26th, covering 2025, is not yet posted as of 2026-08-25.

obligations.who_owes: Sunshine Ordinance Task Force
obligations.deadline_rule: At least once annually

facts.fact: NO existing San Francisco tracker of city compliance with mandated reports or statutory deadlines was found — not at the Controller, the Board, SPUR, GrowSF, TogetherSF, Mission Local, SF Standard, SF Public Press, or the SF Chronicle. Every SF product found tracks service outcomes, promises, or permits; none tracks whether a legally required document was filed by its legal due date. This is a genuine gap.

The Controller's City Performance Scorecards cover 9 service areas (Public Health, Livability, Safety Net, Public Safety, Homelessness, Transportation, Environment, Economy, Finance) with 60+ selected measures and 800+ metrics queryable via DataSF, color-coded against targets. Run by the Controller's Office (Natasha Mihal, Director of City Performance). They measure outcomes, not statutory compliance.

The Scorecards were paused during the pandemic and 'relaunched and fully updated for the first time since early 2020.' The city's own flagship public dashboard went stale for roughly three years — direct evidence that update cadence, not visual design, is the failure mode for civic dashboards. SF Standard also noted the homelessness scorecard depends on data 'only performed every two years' (the PIT count).

GROUND TRUTH SOURCE for this project: HSH's 'Additional Reporting and Compliance' resource collection lists each report HSH submits to the Board with a publication date AND a citation to the mandating authority (e.g. 'In accordance with Ordinance 069-24', 'In accordance with Admin Code Section 10.100-305'). As of 2026-08-25 it contains ZERO occurrences of 'Chapter 124', 'Shelter Equity', or 'equitable distribution'. This is the single most citable negative available for the Sec 124.2(a) Shelter Equity Analysis.

HSH's reports hub describes five buckets: Homelessness Response System Data, Point-in-Time Counts, Homelessness Response System Reports, Additional Reporting and Compliance, and Archived Reports. HSH's previous website was archived on October 21, 2024, so pre-2024 filings live on hsh.archive.sf.gov and post-2024 on sf.gov — a tracker must poll both.

MAJOR CONTEXT: Ordinance 137-26 (File 250630), sponsored by Mandelman and Dorsey but originated in the City Attorney's office, was FINALLY PASSED 7/21/2026 and approved by the Mayor 7/23/2026. It is 362 pages, removes ~150 code sections and modifies 111 enumerated categories of reporting requirements across the Administrative, Environment, Health, Labor, Park, Planning, Police, Public Works, Subdivision, Transportation and BIC Codes.

Item 38 of Ordinance 137-26 is 'Navigation Centers.' The underlying Admin Code Ch. 106 language reads: 'The Controller shall summarize these outcomes in a report to be submitted to the Board of Supervisors no later than within six months of the effective date of this Chapter 106, and every six months thereafter, until such time as the Navigation Centers are no longer in operation.' That is the same six-month/every-six-months shape as Chapter 124 Sec 124.4 — the closest available precedent for how SF treats a semiannual shelter reporting mandate over time.

Chapter 124 (Equitable Distribution of Shelter) was NOT touched by Ordinance 137-26. Verified by extracting the full 19,520-line ordinance text with pdftotext and grepping: zero hits for 'Chapter 124', 'Shelter Equity', or the pattern '124.[0-9]'. The Sec 124.2(a) and Sec 124.4 obligations survive the 2026 cleanup intact.

Board President Mandelman, on the record about mandated reports: 'Many of those reports end up being read by no one.' He also noted that if staffers do not produce the reports, no matter how unnecessary, 'they are technically violating the city's code.' Clerk of the Board Angela Calvillo objected that the digest did not describe every change: 'There is a deviation from the norm... There is a detriment to the public when so many items are combined into such a document.' Supervisor Melgar said she ran the ordinance through Claude to understand it. Ordinance 137-26 was built with Stanford's RegLab using AI to find redundancies, then manually reviewed by City Attorney staff.

MISSION LOCAL LURIE TRACKER — mechanics. datePublished 2025-05-26T18:59:00Z, dateModified 2025-05-28T23:59:13Z. It has NOT been updated since May 2025 despite closing with 'Mission Local will continue to track Lurie's progress... Check back on this page to see Lurie's progress.' All figures frozen at 'As of May 23, 2025': 420 beds announced (28% to goal), 122 opened, 1,080 yet to be rolled out.

Mission Local tracker presentation: three third-party embeds — a Flourish chart (visualisation/23360883), a Flourish table (visualisation/23378822), and a Datawrapper map (chart id XZ0N2, iframe src datawrapper.dwcdn.net/XZ0N2/5/, titled 'Lurie's 1,500-bed goal: 420 announced, 28 percent to goal'). The Datawrapper URL is at version 5, so the chart was revised five times. Design consequence: the prose and the charts can drift out of sync, and the whole thing dies if nobody re-publishes the Flourish/Datawrapper source.

Mission Local's methodology, and the parts worth stealing: (1) a dual counter separating ANNOUNCED from OPENED; (2) breakdown by bed type — 68 homeless shelter, 76 short-term medical/stabilization (30-60 days), 182 longer-term recovery housing, 94 treatment; (3) net-of-replacement accounting, explicitly flagging that 57 of the treatment beds 'will replace 97 current beds at the Behavioral Health Center' — i.e. a net LOSS of 40, which a naive counter would score as +57; (4) geographic distribution by supervisorial district, noting only one site (68 beds, Marina) sits outside the eastern neighborhoods; (5) explicit tracking of definition drift — Lurie's March 2025 executive directive both moved the deadline from June to mid-September and redefined 'shelter bed' to include 'hotel vouchers, transitional housing, stabilization centers, recovery and sober housing, and residential treatment.'

Mission Local published an in-page correction: 'The number of beds open as of initial publication should have been 122 instead of 54.' Corrections live inside the tracker page rather than in a separate log — a cheap, credible pattern worth copying.

The tracker died before the promise did. SF Standard reported (Jan 2026) that Lurie officially dropped the 1,500-bed pledge in July 2025 and that roughly 500 beds were created in 2025 — twice the time he gave himself for three times the number. Mission Local's page still shows 420/28% from May 2025. The lesson: a promise tracker that stops updating becomes evidence against the tracker, not the official.

BEST STRUCTURAL ANALOGUE: ProPublica's Transparency Tracker monitored whether federal agencies complied with a White House OMB directive of Dec 8, 2009 requiring open-government websites by Feb 6, 2010. Columns: agency name, 'Live?' status, and 'First Seen' timestamp. This is the same shape as Chapter 124 — a dated legal mandate, a specific artifact owed, a fixed due date.

How ProPublica handled the 'we could not find it' problem, four moves worth copying verbatim: (1) exploit a predictable URL convention (the directive specified www.agency.gov/open) so absence is mechanically checkable rather than a judgment call; (2) hedge in the methodology — 'there may be open government sites we couldn't find'; (3) crowdsource the correction — 'Please let us know if we missed one'; (4) publish failures loudly — a programming error mis-reported posting dates for five agencies (HUD, Interior, Treasury, NASA, VA), which were then relabeled 'N/A (see correction)' rather than silently fixed. Note also that 'First Seen' is a machine-observed timestamp, a claim about what the crawler saw and when, NOT a claim about when the agency posted — that framing is what survived the correction.

PolitiFact promise-meter status taxonomy (Trump-O-Meter, now MAGA-Meter): Promise Kept, Promise Broken, Compromise, Stalled, In the Works, Not Yet Rated. 'Stalled' means no movement, 'perhaps because of limitations on money, opposition from lawmakers or a shift in priorities.' Two design rules: ratings are based on verifiable outcomes, not intentions or effort; and ratings are explicitly REVERSIBLE — a promise can go In the Works, fall back to Stalled, then return to In the Works. A tracker needs a state meaning 'nothing is happening' that is distinct from 'broken', and states must be allowed to move backwards.

MuckRock uses seven request statuses: Awaiting Response, Awaiting Appeal, Fix Required, Payment Required, Rejected, No Responsive Documents, and Completed. 'No Responsive Documents' is its own status, distinct from Rejected and from Awaiting Response. The critical modeling lesson: 'the agency told us it does not exist', 'we searched and could not find it', and 'we have not asked yet' are three different facts and must never collapse into one red cell.

MuckRock's FOIA FAQ on agencies claiming no records exist when they do: agencies are required to perform a 'reasonable' search, 'reasonable' is relative, and agencies sometimes conduct inadequate searches. Their recommendation is to go back to the agency explaining why records should exist. For a tracker, this means a 'department says no such report exists' cell should carry the department's exact wording and the date it was said, not a paraphrase.

Chicago PD's Consent Decree Compliance Dashboard is the best deadline-compliance UI model: paragraph-level compliance status for each requirement, filterable by status, with each paragraph expandable to show the requirement's literal language beside its compliance status and the monitor's feedback. It updates semi-annually, deliberately pinned to the Independent Monitoring Team's semi-annual report cadence. Two lessons: pin your refresh cadence to the source document's cadence rather than inventing your own, and show the mandate text next to the status so a reader can audit your reading of it.

The journalistic counterpart to a compliance dashboard: Chicago Sun-Times, 'City missed 40% of police consent-decree deadlines last year.' A percentage-of-deadlines-missed headline number is the reportable artifact a deadline tracker produces. Worth designing that number in from the start.

COVID Tracking Project graded all 56 states and territories weekly on data quality using 16 factors across 5 categories, producing a letter grade. They then deliberately RETIRED the letter grades in favor of 'a more granular set of annotations' because states kept changing their reporting and the researchers learned more about why data was or wasn't reported. Lesson: a single compressed grade invites arguments about the grade instead of the underlying gap; per-item annotations are more defensible and age better. They also sunset the project deliberately with a documented archive rather than letting it rot.

PROVING A NEGATIVE — the legal doctrine. California Evidence Code § 1284: a writing made by the public employee who is the official custodian of records 'reciting diligent search and failure to find a record' is not made inadmissible by the hearsay rule when offered to prove the absence of a record in that office. The federal analogues are FRE 803(7) (absence of a record of a regularly conducted activity) and FRE 803(10) (absence of a public record). The operative legal standard is a DILIGENT SEARCH, documented — not certainty.

PROVING A NEGATIVE — the evidentiary test to design around: absence is probative only where the matter 'is of a type that the records would regularly include' and the source or circumstances do not indicate a lack of trustworthiness. Practically this means the tracker must first establish that this kind of report is normally published in this place, and only then treat its absence there as meaningful. The counterweight, stated plainly in the same guidance: an absence of records is not proof nothing happened.

Practical translation for the site's language: never write 'HSH did not produce the report.' Write 'No published Shelter Equity Analysis was found at [list of specific URLs checked] as of [timestamp],' with the search log (URL, HTTP status, timestamp) exposed, the custodian contacted and the date, and an invitation to correct. That is the ProPublica hedge plus the Cal. Evid. Code § 1284 diligent-search standard, combined.

GrowSF has announced a permit performance tracker (permitting throughput, not statutory report compliance). Relevant supporting anecdote: when GrowSF co-founder Steven Bacio's team embedded in the Planning Department, they could not answer 'how many homes have been approved' because the data did not exist in usable form — planners used permit tracking systems as time-tracking systems. Useful precedent that SF civic-tech accountability projects routinely discover the source data was never structured for the question.

The Controller's City Services Auditor (Audits Division + City Performance Division, funded by a charter-mandated 0.2% of the >$9B budget) does performance, financial and COMPLIANCE auditing of departments and runs the whistleblower program. However, the Library cannot guarantee the permanence of these URLs. The online documents they link to may be moved or removed from a Web site or server without the Library receiving notification.' The city's official compliance registry is therefore annual-reports-only, incomplete, and link-rot-prone — which is the argument for building this tracker with archived snapshots rather than live links.

Penal Code 933(c) verbatim: "No later than 90 days after the grand jury submits a final report on the operations of any public agency subject to its reviewing authority, the governing body of the public agency shall comment to the presiding judge of the superior court on the findings and recommendations pertaining to matters under the control of the governing body, and every elected county officer or agency head for which the grand jury has responsibility pursuant to Section 914.1 shall comment within 60 days to the presiding judge of the superior court, with an information copy sent to the board of supervisors... In any city and county, the mayor shall also comment on the findings and recommendations." Last amended by Stats. 2002, Ch. 784, Sec. 538, effective January 1, 2003.

The 90-day clock in 933(c) runs from when the grand jury SUBMITS the final report, not from publication. San Francisco practice collapses this: the Jury's own tables state "within 60 calendar days" / "within 90 calendar days" and BOS Resolution 480-24 recites "within 90 days of receipt." sf.gov's "Published" date is the practical anchor for computing due dates.

Penal Code 933.05 fixes the required response FORM, which makes responses machine-checkable. Per finding: (1) agrees, or (2) disagrees wholly or partially, specifying the disputed portion with reasons. Per recommendation: (1) implemented, with summary; (2) not yet implemented but will be, with a timeframe; (3) requires further analysis, with scope and a timeframe that "shall not exceed six months from the date of publication of the grand jury report"; (4) will not be implemented because not warranted or not reasonable, with explanation. Amended by Stats. 1997, Ch. 443, Sec. 5, effective January 1, 1998.

933.05(f): the Jury must give the affected agency the portion of the report relating to it two working days before public release; no officer, agency, department, or governing body may disclose report contents before public release. 933.05(c): where a finding touches budgetary or personnel matters of an agency headed by an elected officer, both the head and the board of supervisors respond if requested, but the board's response addresses only matters over which it has decisionmaking authority.

Penal Code 914.1, the cross-reference that scopes who owes the 60-day response, is only about the judge's charge to the grand jury at impanelment (Gov. Code 23000 et seq., 24054, 26525, etc.). It contains no list of covered officers or agency heads, so "agency head for which the grand jury has responsibility" is not crisply defined by the statute. 933(d) says only that "agency" includes a department.

"At Scale, At Risk: Upgrading Data and Oversight to Improve Homelessness Services" — SF Civil Grand Jury 2025-2026, cover date June 23, 2026, 5 findings, 15 recommendations. F1: HSH has not used Critical Incident Reports effectively to identify troubling patterns or improve safety at housing sites. F2: HSH lags in presenting data allowing benchmarking of nonprofits by program or housing type, and in using data to trigger automated targeted monitoring. F3: HSH's cessation of submitting certain contracts to HOC for review and consent, and of notifying HOC of renewals/extensions as line items, undermines HOC as a governing oversight body. F4: HOC has not exercised the full extent of its statutory authority and lacks training and resources. F5: the Shelter Monitoring Committee is set to terminate by a recent ordinance and HSH has insufficient resources to absorb its work or oversee PSH sites effectively.

Recommendation deadlines inside "At Scale, At Risk" (jury-set targets, not statutory, and only binding to the extent a respondent accepts them): By December 2026 — R1.1 CIR dashboard updated at least monthly, filterable by coded incident (deaths, overdoses, acts/threats of violence, sexual assault, denial of service), provider, housing type, zip, year; R1.2 redesignate HSH Program Compliance as "Safety and Compliance" with quarterly safety reporting to HOC; R2.1 publish performance dashboards aligned to the Performance Measurement Plan; R3.1 return contract renewals and extensions to HOC's consent calendar; R3.2 HSH and HOC set new thresholds for HOC contract review; R5.1 and R5.2 Controller reviews of what HSH needs to absorb SMC's functions and to run unannounced PSH site visits. By March 2027 — R2.2 internal benchmarking of providers for performance/safety outliers; R4.2 revise the Executive Director's monthly HOC report; R4.3 HOC initiates or commissions a performance audit of overdoses (including reversals) and deaths at PSH sites. By June 2027 — R1.3 aggregated CIR data in the Director's quarterly HOC report and a public dashboard; R4.1 City Attorney onboarding/training materials for HOC. By December 2027 — R1.4 a "Safety Standards" section in all HSH nonprofit contracts with thresholds triggering targeted review; R2.3 data-driven automation alerts for triggering contract review.

R5.1 and R5.2 are the two recommendations that bear directly on shelter/PSH oversight: by December 2026 the Controller's Office should report on what changes and resources would let HSH carry on the Shelter Monitoring Committee's functions, and separately on what it would take for HSH to implement unannounced site visits and other monitoring changes at permanent supportive housing sites. The report's note to Finding 5 states that SMC was the only independent body empowered to conduct unannounced site visits to City-funded shelters for Standards of Care monitoring, staffed by two DPH full-time employees, that its mandate never extended to PSH, and that on the ordinance's effective date "there will be no independent body authorized to conduct unannounced inspections of City-funded homeless services facilities of any kind — neither shelters nor PSH," with the complaint investigation function moving to HSH.

The ordinance that abolishes the Shelter Monitoring Committee and the Shelter Grievance Advisory Committee is Board File No. 260217 / Ordinance No. 99-26, "[Various Codes - Boards, Commissions, and Advisory Bodies]", from the Commission Streamlining Task Force. Rules Committee referred it without recommendation May 4, 2026; passed first reading May 12, 2026 (6-4, Ayes Dorsey, Mahmood, Mandelman, Sauter, Sherrill, Wong; Noes Chan, Chen, Melgar, Walton; Excused Fielder); FINALLY PASSED May 19, 2026 on the same 6-4 vote. api.sf.gov exposes a public, unauthenticated Wagtail API v2. `curl -s 'https://api.sf.gov/api/v2/pages/'` returns HTTP 200 application/json with meta.total_count = 94255. `curl -s 'https://api.sf.gov/api/v2/documents/'` returns total_count = 58890. This is the CMS backing sf.gov and is by far the best detection substrate found.

New-document detection recipe that works: `curl -s 'https://api.sf.gov/api/v2/documents/?order=-id&limit=1000&fields=title,created_at'`. Returns id, title, created_at, meta.download_url (api.sf.gov/documents/<id>/<file>) and file (media.api.sf.gov/documents/<file>). Newest id observed 2026-08-25 was 62467.

Document velocity is 40-200 new documents/day city-wide. A single limit=1000 descending-id poll spans 18 days (ids 61409 to 62467 covering 2026-07-31 to 2026-08-24), so a daily cron has enormous slack and even a weekly run would not miss anything.

The pages endpoint supports typed filtering, which gives a precise 'a new report was published' signal: type=sf.Report (5,547 pages), sf.Meeting (30,384), sf.News (12,209), sf.Information (11,554), sf.Agency, sf.ResourceCollection. Working call: `curl -s 'https://api.sf.gov/api/v2/pages/?type=sf.Report&order=-id&limit=200&fields=title,first_published_at'`.

Wagtail API full-text search works on both endpoints: `?search=shelter` on /pages/ returns total=233; `?search=shelter%20equity` on /documents/ returns total=2. Search is AND-based across terms, so an over-long phrase returns 0 rather than fuzzy matches.

Order Wagtail results by -id, never by dates. `order=-last_published_at` and `order=-latest_revision_created_at` are rejected with {"message": "cannot order by '-last_published_at' (unknown field)"}. `order=-first_published_at` is accepted but sorts nulls first and returns items whose meta.first_published_at is null. Also, combining `search=` with `order=` returns an error object with no meta key.

Wagtail document created_at is the upload timestamp and is reliable; published_date is an editor-typed field and is garbage. Document id 6275 carries published_date '2222-02-02'; document id 60248 has created_at 2026-07-06 but published_date 2026-03-18. Key off created_at or id.

sf.gov/sitemap.xml works as a secondary diff source: HTTP 200, application/xml, 8,775,871 bytes, 17,253 <loc> entries each with a <lastmod> date. Freshness confirmed: max lastmod was 2026-08-24 when fetched 2026-08-25. Keyword prefilter on shelter/homeless/behavioral/equity/real-estate narrows it to 582 URLs. Translations appear as separate /es/, /fil/, /zh-hant/, /vi-vn/ URLs and should be filtered out.

The sitemap sends NO ETag and NO Last-Modified header (only cache-control: public, max-age=600), so conditional GET is impossible and every poll pulls the full 8.8MB. This is the main reason to prefer the Wagtail API.

sf.gov search: the working query parameter is `q=`, NOT `search_api_fulltext=`. Results are server-rendered into the page's __NEXT_DATA__ JSON blob under props.pageProps.results, backed by Google Vertex AI Search (datastore sfgov-data_1725089961554). Each result has derivedStructData.title, .link and .datePublished. It indexes PDFs on media.api.sf.gov and sites/default/files as well as HTML pages.

A clean JSON search endpoint exists at https://www.sf.gov/_next/data/<buildId>/en/search.json?q=<terms> (HTTP 200, application/json, ~148KB). buildId was WKDrj02k9AXPIuWeDIVuu on 2026-08-25 and rotates on every deploy; a stale buildId returns HTTP 404. Scraping __NEXT_DATA__ from the plain HTML page is more durable than chasing buildId.

Socrata discovery catalog works but has a silent-failure trap: `search_context=data.sfgov.org` is MANDATORY. Without it, `?domains=data.sfgov.org&order=updatedAt&limit=100` returns resultSetSize 5 and 5 rows with no error. With it, resultSetSize is 1218 and limit honours values up to at least 1000.

For detecting NEW DataSF datasets use `order=createdAt+DESC`, not updatedAt. updatedAt reflects data refreshes on live feeds (Law Enforcement Dispatched Calls, 911 Shots Fired) and churns every few minutes, producing a rolling window that generated 24 false positives on a second run minutes later. createdAt DESC was stable across runs; newest dataset created was qbrs-bfjk on 2026-08-04.

Socrata `only=` filtering is useless on this domain: only=dataset returns 4, only=map returns 1, and only=chart/filter/href/calendar/file/document/link/story/measure/datalens all return 0, against a true total of 1218. Do not filter by asset type.

media.api.sf.gov is a CloudFront-fronted S3 bucket. Exact-object GET works (https://media.api.sf.gov/images/2026_PIT_Count_Completing_Assessment_May_2026.original.png returns HTTP 200 image/png 185691 bytes) but listing is denied: /, /documents, /api, and ?list-type=2&prefix=documents/ all return HTTP 403 with AccessDenied, server: AmazonS3. Fetch-by-exact-URL only, which is why the Wagtail documents endpoint matters, it is the index media.api does not provide.

https://www.sf.gov/documents/<id>/<filename> 307-redirects to https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/<filename>. Confirmed with -L: sf.gov/documents/47792/Equity_Analysis_-_Executive_Summary.pdf resolves to media.api.sf.gov/documents/Equity_Analysis_-_Executive_Summary.pdf, HTTP 200, application/pdf, 176952 bytes.

Commission agenda URL patterns on sf.gov are inconsistent and cannot be predicted reliably. Health Commission uses a full-date double slug: /meeting--august-3-2026--august-3-2026-health-commission-meeting. Homelessness Oversight Commission changed format for 2026 to month-only: /meeting--august-2026-homelessness-oversight-commission-meeting, whereas 2025 used /meeting--august-7-2025-homelessness-oversight-commission-meeting. SF is a per-department system. The central portal sanfrancisco.nextrequest.com accepts requests for 18 participating departments: ADM (Office of the City Administrator), Animal Care and Control, Arts Commission, Building Inspection, Controller, Department of Public Health, Department of Technology, Ethics Commission, Fire Department, Homelessness and Supportive Housing, Human Rights Commission, Library, Office of Contract Administration, PUC, Public Works, SFMTA, Recreation & Parks, and Treasurer & Tax Collector. The portal states verbatim: "If you have a request for a department not on that list, visit that department's website and follow the instructions there for submitting a request. Requests submitted through this portal for non-participating departments will be closed out." It also requires a separate request per department.

NextRequest requests are PUBLIC and citable. 15,942 published requests as of 2026-08-25. Each has a stable path /requests/{pretty_id} such as /requests/25-9723, and the listing carries request_date, due_date, request_state (Open/Closed/Overdue), department_names, poc_name and the full request text. This is exactly the data a deadline tracker needs and it is already public.

Undocumented but working NextRequest JSON API on the SF instance, no auth required. GET /client/requests?page=N returns {total_count, requests[]}. GET /client/requests?page=1&search_term=shelter does full-text search. GET /client/requests?page=1&department_ids[]=12466 filters by department (note: department_ids[] works, department_id and departments[] are silently ignored and return everything). GET /client/departments returns the 26 request queues with numeric ids. GET /client/requests/{pretty_id} returns request metadata. GET /client/requests/{pretty_id}/timeline returns the full public event log including staff response text and closure letters. GET /client/documents?page=1&search_term=X searches 619,225 released documents.

Key NextRequest department ids for this project: HOM - Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing = 12466 (only 9 published requests, all Nov-Dec 2025). ADM = 14911 (21 published requests, latest 01/02/2025). DPH is split across 12 queues, the general one being "Public Health: Other" = 79. There is no Planning queue and no separate Real Estate queue.

HSH records-request destination is HSHsunshine@sfgov.org. HSH is also a NextRequest participating department, and HSH staff sign off closure letters on the portal with "reach out via NextRequest or email at hshsunshine@sfgov.org". Filing via NextRequest is strictly better for the tracker because it produces a public, citable request ID and a public due date.

Real Estate Division records-request destination is admsunshinerequests@sfgov.org. RED sits under the City Administrator, so it can alternatively be filed on NextRequest under the "ADM" queue. SOTF's 2025 Annual Report lists "ADM- Real Estate (0)" among bodies included in the NextRequest summary report that received zero records requests in 2025, so this is an untouched queue.

DPH publishes its own deadline page stating: 10 calendar days to respond, plus up to 14 calendar days extension with written notice inside the first 10 days explaining why and giving an estimated response date. For an Immediate Disclosure Request, DPH "must respond to these requests by the close of the next business day". Three channels: NextRequest, email to DPH.sunshine@sfdph.org titled "Immediate Disclosure Request", or mail to Custodian of Public Records, Department of Public Health, 1145 Market Street, SF, CA 94103 with the words across the top of the request and on the envelope.

Planning is NOT on NextRequest. Requests go by email to CPC-RecordRequest@sfgov.org, using the department's PDF form at https://sfplanning.org/sites/default/files/forms/PublicRecordRequest_Form.pdf, or by fax to 415.558.6377. Page last updated 05/10/2026. There is no public log of Planning requests, so the tracker cannot cite a Planning request ID and must self-host the evidence (sent-mail timestamp, form copy).

Board of Supervisors records requests go to board.of.supervisors@sfgov.org. Since the Sec. 124.4 semiannual report is submitted TO the Board, the cheapest first check is Legistar for a Clerk file, not a records request.

Machine-readable trick for finding any SF department's records-request destination: every sf.gov department page renders a standardized block with an anchor carrying data-testid="public-records-link". Grep the HTML of https://www.sf.gov/departments--{slug} for that attribute and the href is the department's actual submission target (mailto or portal URL). Verified on HSH, Real Estate Division, and Board of Supervisors.

Sec. 67.25(a) verbatim IDR text: "Notwithstanding the 10-day period for response to a request permitted in Government Code Section 6256 and in this Article, a written request for information described in any category of non-exempt public information shall be satisfied no later than the close of business on the day following the day of the request. This deadline shall apply only if the words 'Immediate Disclosure Request' are placed across the top of the request and on the envelope, subject line, or cover sheet in which the request is transmitted. Maximum deadlines provided in this article are appropriate for more extensive or demanding requests, but shall not be used to delay fulfilling a simple, routine or otherwise readily answerable request." The Gov. Code cross-reference (6256) is to the pre-1998 CPRA numbering and is stale in the ordinance itself.

Sec. 67.25(b) verbatim: "If the voluminous nature of the information requested, its location in a remote storage facility or the need to consult with another interested department warrants an extension of 10 days as provided in Government Code Section 6456.1, the requester shall be notified as required by the close of business on the business day following the request." 6456.1 does not exist and is almost certainly a scrivener's error for the repealed 6256.1. The live CPRA cap is 14 days under 7922.535(b). Chapter 67 itself therefore never expressly grants a 14-day extension for an ordinary 67.21(b) request; departments import it from the CPRA via 67.21(k).

Sunshine Ordinance Task Force complaint filing. Online form: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSe6X8DJ0CW6cE8PLGQeypyJUjODjOgH5WmRwz44fRSJHvtdlg/viewform. Downloadable PDF form and instructions (adopted 11-3-2015): https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/53444-Complain_Form_and_Instructions_-_Adopted_11-3-2015.pdf. Also accepted by email to sotf@sfgov.org, fax 415-554-5163, or in person at City Hall Room 244, 1 Dr. Carlton B. Goodlett Place, SF CA 94102-4683. Phone 415-554-7724. sf.gov tells you to contact SOTF first for informal resolution. Complaints are public record; to stay anonymous you must self-anonymize because SOTF does not redact.

SOTF meeting cadence, which drives the real complaint clock: Full Task Force meets the 1st Wednesday of the month at 4:00 p.m.; the Complaint Committee (which actually hears complaints first) meets the 3rd Tuesday at 5:30 p.m.; Compliance and Amendments Committee meets the 4th Tuesday of even months. Clerk: Patricia Petersen, patricia.petersen@sfgov.org, 415-554-7719. Active as of Aug 2026 (Complaint Committee 08/18/26, Full Task Force 08/05/26).

DIRECT PRECEDENT. SOTF File No. 26035, Grant Review v. Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing, decision issued 5/6/2026, order approved 6/3/2026. Complaint alleged violation of 67.21 and 67.25 (failure to respond to a records request and to an Immediate Disclosure Request). SOTF found HSH violated 67.21(b), ordered production under 67.21(e), and ordered specifically: "Operating contract for the following facilities: Medical Respite Center, Hope House, Civic Center Motor Inn, and any records of complaints received from any facilities covered by the public records request." The order notes "the Respondent acknowledged that documents were not provided timely and/or complete manner". Vote 11-0.

DIRECT PRECEDENT. SOTF File No. 26037, Grant Review v. HSH, decision issued 5/6/2026. SOTF found HSH violated Sec. 67.21(c) by failing to provide assistance AND Sec. 67.21(e) by failing to attend the Task Force hearing. It ordered HSH to identify and provide records on program monitoring activities under the Controller's Policy on annual monitoring. A department not showing up to its own hearing is the cleanest illustration of what SOTF lacks.

SOTF 2025 Annual Report (released 2026-03-16) hard numbers: the City received at least 56,178 records requests in 2025. SOTF received 127 new complaints and resolved 61. It found 53 violations across 34 complaints and no violations in 18. Average time to hear a complaint was 138 days, down from 333 in 2024 and 407 in 2023, against a 45-day statutory limit; only 25% were scheduled within 45 days and 63% heard within 100 days. Backlog grew from 20 complaints at the start of 2025 to 60 at the end. Mean fulfilment time was 11 days by department self-report but 33 days per NextRequest data (median 9 days; median initial acknowledgement 1 day).

THE ENFORCEMENT GAP, in SOTF's own words. 2025: 54 orders issued, 20 with directions to monitor compliance, ZERO orders with confirmed compliance, 6 with confirmed noncompliance (SFMTA, SFPD, the Zoo, the Fire Commission), and 2 complaints referred to the DA or Ethics Commission. The report states the ordinance directs SOTF to notify the DA or AG within 5 days of noncompliance, "However, this rarely happens in practice."

Ethics Commission is the terminal dead end for enforcement. On 7/11/2025 it voted to take no action in the SOTF referral Matthew Lotocki v. San Francisco Police Department (File No. 24021), questioning "whether the Commission has statutory authority to impose administrative penalties in connection with SOTF referrals, since such authority is not clearly articulated within the Charter or the Sunshine Ordinance." SOTF's 2025 report adds that Ethics staff proposed revised Enforcement Regulations that would remove its role in enforcing non-willful violations under 67.35(d), and that Ethics has never defined "willful" for 67.34 despite repeated requests.

Ethics Commission procedures for SOTF referrals, from its own page: Section 10(A) hearings cover alleged willful violations by elected officials or department heads, staff investigates, complainant bears the burden. Section 10(B) hearings cover everyone else plus non-willful violations by elected officials or department heads, the respondent bears the burden of proving no violation, and "Commission staff does not prepare any analysis in such matters." Complainants "generally must first notify the District Attorney and/or Attorney General" before filing directly with Ethics. Ethics defers anything still pending at SOTF.

Supervisor of Records is the wrong forum for a missed deadline. The City Attorney's own page states verbatim that the Supervisor of Records "only decides if records are public" and "does not: Decide if responses are timely / Issue violations against City departments." Sec. 67.36 supersession clause, useful when a department cites a narrower local rule: "The provisions of this Sunshine Ordinance supersede other local laws. Whenever a conflict in local law is identified, the requirement which would result in greater or more expedited public access to public information shall apply." Note it addresses conflicts in LOCAL law, so it does not by its terms override the state CPRA 14-day extension.

Sec. 67.21(g) shifts the burden in litigation: "In any court proceeding pursuant to this article there shall be a presumption that the record sought is public, and the burden shall be upon the custodian to prove with specificity the exemption which applies." Sec. 67.28 bars charging personnel costs for responding to a records request, and 67.21(a) caps copy charges at the lesser of actual cost or ten cents per page. A fee demand beyond that is itself flaggable.
City Attorney's Good Government Guide, 2024 edition, is the authoritative city-published overview of the Brown Act, CPRA and Sunshine Ordinance including remedies and penalties. Live PDF, 1.5 MB.

Admin Code Sec. 1.56 is a three-subsection framework with no schedule attached. Its full operative text is: (a) every board or commission shall prepare an annual report describing its activities as part of the Annual Statement of Purpose required under Charter Sec. 4.102(2), containing a general summary of the department's services and programs in terms accessible to the average citizen plus highlights of the prior year; (b) reports must be posted on the City's official website and the URL transmitted to the Documents Department of SFPL within 10 days of final approval, with SFPL maintaining a directory of URLs; (c) where no date is otherwise specified by law, each body must inform the Clerk of the Board in writing of the date by which it will annually post. There is NO list of departments and NO list of named reports — the brief's premise that Sec. 1.56 enumerates homelessness/health-relevant entries is wrong.

Charter Sec. 4.133 (Homelessness Oversight Commission, added by Prop C, approved 11/8/2022) contains NO reporting cadence and NO report deadline. Its powers under (f)(1) are the generic Charter 4.102/4.103/4.104 commission powers plus 'conducting performance audits of the Department to assess the efficiency and effectiveness of the Department's delivery of services ... and the extent to which the Department has met the annual goals and performance standards established by the Commission' — with no interval specified for those audits. Under (f)(2) the Commission may NOT approve, disapprove, or modify eligibility or priority criteria for programs where those criteria are a condition of state or federal funding.

Divisions (h)-(j) of Charter Sec. 4.133, as added by Prop C (11/8/2022), expired on April 17, 2024 under their own sunset provision and were removed from the Charter at the direction of the Office of the City Attorney. Their content is not visible in the current codified Charter. If Prop C's HOC reporting or transition duties lived anywhere, they lived here — worth recovering from the Prop C legal text.

Timeline anchors for the HOC: initial appointments to Seats 1-7 were due by noon March 1, 2023; the Commission came into existence upon appointment of four members or at noon May 1, 2023, whichever was later; its inaugural meeting was due within 30 days of coming into existence; commissioners serve four-year terms beginning noon May 1, 2023, except initial Seats 1, 4 and 6 which were two-year terms expiring noon May 1, 2025.

'Home by the Bay' is a VOLUNTARY departmental strategic plan, not a legally mandated document with statutory dates. Admin Code Sec. 2A.410, which creates HSH (Added by Ord. 116-16, File No. 160638, App. 6/29/2016; amended by Ord. 35-23), assigns the Department duties to manage housing/programs/services and to staff the HOC and the Local Homeless Coordinating Board, and nothing more — no strategic plan, no report, no deadline. Charter Sec. 4.133 imposes none either. The only statutory acknowledgment that a plan exists is oblique: Bus. & Tax Reg. Code Sec. 2810(e)(2)(B) says the OCOH needs assessment 'shall inform the Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing's strategic planning process,' and Admin Code Sec. 5.41-2(d) repeats that each needs assessment 'shall be transmitted to the Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing to inform the Department's strategic planning process.' Presupposing a process is not mandating a plan on a clock. Treat Home by the Bay progress reports (Year One, Oct. 2024; Year Two, presented to the HOC on 11/21/2025) as discretionary departmental publications.

The 'Fentanyl State of Emergency Ordinance' is Ordinance No. 10-25, Board File No. 250040, formally titled '[Administrative Code - Core Initiatives to Strengthen City's Responses to Homelessness, Drug Abuse, Mental Health Needs, and Related Crises]'. Approved 2/12/2025; per amlegal the code amendments are Eff. 3/15/2025 (the Board's own ordinance index lists 2/12/2025 for Section 4 and 3/14/2025 for all sections; Ord. Sec. 6 makes the behested-payments waiver section effective immediately on enactment and everything else 30 days after enactment). It rewrote Admin Code Chapter 21B, which had existed since Ord. 61-19 (File No. 190047, 2019) and was previously amended by Ord. 38-24.

The Fentanyl emergency ordinance carries NO report-back-or-renew clock in the classic emergency-declaration sense. Its accountability mechanism is Sec. 21B.6(b) quarterly contract reporting plus Sec. 21B.4 annual donations reporting. Chapter 21B expires by operation of law on May 5, 2029 (Sec. 21B.7), and Ord. 10-25 STRUCK the alternative trigger that would have ended the chapter early upon a Board finding that the Point-in-Time count showed no more than 2,199 people experiencing unsheltered homelessness (a 50% reduction from the 2022 count). Several sub-authorities lapsed on their own: non-competitive award authority for non-homelessness Core Initiative Contracts and Leases ended January 8, 2026 (Secs. 21B.3(b)(2), (b)(3)); the Charter Sec. 9.118 delegation to the Mayor required the resolution to be introduced on or before January 8, 2026 (Sec. 21B.3(c)(1)); the donation authority ended January 8, 2026 (Sec. 21B.4); and the unrestricted intra-department transfer authority ended January 8, 2026 (Sec. 21B.5).

Chapter 21B's 45-day 'shot clock' is real and precisely drawn: under Sec. 21B.3(c)(6) the Mayor may approve a Core Initiative Contract or Lease in writing only if the Board fails to act within 45 days after the Clerk publishes the introduced legislation, with the 45 days tolled while the resolution is referred to Planning for a CEQA determination and while the Board is on regular recess. Ceilings: under $25 million in anticipated expenditure and under a ten-year term, with carve-outs for affordable housing ground leases (up to 99 years), affordable housing loans, and rent/operating subsidy grants (up to 30 years).

Ordinance 99-26, File No. 260217, App. 5/29/2026, Eff. 6/29/2026 — '[Various Codes - Boards, Commissions, and Advisory Bodies]', sponsored by the Commission Streamlining Task Force and Supervisor Mandelman — is a very recent omnibus that reshaped this whole space. It defines and distinguishes Commissions from Advisory Bodies, sets four-year terms with three-term limits for Commissions and three-year terms with four-term limits for Advisory Bodies, modifies sunset dates, abolishes certain bodies, and consolidates most bodies into Admin Code Chapter 5. Directly relevant effects I confirmed: it REPEALED Ch. 20, Art. XII 'Shelter Monitoring Committee' (former Secs. 20.300 through 20.312); it amended every section of the Our City, Our Home Oversight Committee article (Admin Code Secs. 5.41-1 through 5.41-4); and it relocated the Local Homeless Coordinating Board into Chapter 5 as Article XXXI (Secs. 5.31-1 et seq.).

The Shelter Monitoring Committee no longer exists in the Administrative Code. The amlegal editor's note reads: 'Ch. 20, Art. XII, "Shelter Monitoring Committee," comprising Secs. 20.300 through 20.312, was repealed by Ord. 99-26.' Sec. 20.400(a) still recites the 2004 finding that the Board 'created the Shelter Monitoring Committee that is required to provide the Mayor, the Board of Supervisors, and others with accurate and comprehensive information about the conditions in and operations of shelters,' and Sec. 20.405 still contains a mangled residual reference ('The Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing Shelter Monitoring Committee shall also forward the results of its investigation to the Director'), flagged by the publisher as a codification note. Any tracker built on SMC reporting is now tracking a dead body — but the shelter complaint clocks in Sec. 20.405 survive: staff acknowledge receipt within 2 business days, respond in writing within 5 business days, HSH investigates within 10 business days of a client request, and the Director must comply with Sec. 20.406(a) within 45 days.

The Our City, Our Home Oversight Committee is created by Admin Code Secs. 5.41-1 through 5.41-4 (Ch. 5, Art. XLI), added by Ord. 51-19, File No. 181210, App. 3/22/2019, Eff. 4/22/2019, and amended by Ord. 23-23, Ord. 35-23 and Ord. 99-26. It has nine voting members and must hold a regular meeting not less than six times per fiscal year (Sec. 5.41-4(a)). Representatives from HSH, MOHCD, the Controller and DPH must attend all regular meetings. Notwithstanding Board Rule 2.21 (three-year advisory-body sunsets), the Committee does not expire unless the Board enacts a terminating ordinance (Sec. 5.41-4(d)).

Board File No. 250487 is Ordinance No. 172-25, effective 10/6/2025, and its OFFICIAL TITLE in the Board's own 2025 ordinance index is 'Administrative Code - Equitable Citywide Access to Shelters, Transitional Housing, and Behavioral Health Services' — which differs from the Chapter 124 heading 'Equitable Distribution of Shelter, Transitional Housing, and Behavioral Health Facilities' given in the brief. Ordinance 300-19 (Mental Health SF, File No. 191148, App. 12/20/2019) split its own effective dates: the ordinance took effect 30 days after enactment (1/20/2020); Section 2 (Article XLIV, the Implementation Working Group) became operative on that effective date; but Section 1 (Sec. 15.104, Mental Health SF itself) was made operative only on the earliest of three conditions in Sec. 3(b) — a Controller certification that the City budget exceeded the prior year's by 13%, a Controller certification that voters approved a tax yielding revenue sufficient to finance Sec. 15.104, or the City enacting an appropriation ordinance sufficiently financing Mental Health SF. Every Sec. 15.104 report deadline except the Feb. 1 Implementation Plan is keyed to that unresolved operative date.

Former Sec. 5.44-3 (IWG membership) was amended by Ord. 109-24, File No. 240281, App. 6/6/2024, Eff. 7/7/2024, and former Sec. 5.44-5 (the sunset) was amended by Ord. 295-24, File No. 240984, App. 12/19/2024, Eff. 1/19/2025 — the same date the Article expired. Admin Code Chapter 20 as currently codified contains these articles relevant to this lane: XI Street Teams Reports; XIII Standard of Care for City Shelters; XIV Tenant Eviction Annual Reports; XV CAAP Discontinuance Rental Assistance Pilot Project; XVI Coordinated Entry System; Prioritization and Coordination of Care for Persons Discharged from Residential Behavioral Health Programs; XVIII Shelter Grievance Policy; XIX Homeward Bound Program; XX Cash Not Drugs Pilot Program; XXI Rapid Rehousing Program. The Local Homeless Coordinating Board, as rewritten by Ord. 99-26 into Admin Code Ch. 5, Art. XXXI, has 11 members appointed by the Homelessness Oversight Commission (Seat 1 a homeless or formerly homeless person; Seats 2-11 representing relevant organizations or homeless subpopulations as those terms are used in the federal CoC regulation cited in the ordinance text).
